function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a CI script) to finish the whole workflow.  
I’ll also give you ready‑to‑use templates for the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests and GitHub Actions workflow so you can drop them into the repo right away.

> **NOTE** – I can’t actually clone or push the repo for you, but the commands below will do it on your machine (or in a CI runner).  
> If you’re running this in a CI environment that already has the repo checked out, just skip the `git clone` step.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you’re already inside the repo, you can skip the `git clone` line.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Analyse the repo

We’ll use the `analyse_repo_contents` helper to get a quick overview of the dominant language(s).  
(If you don’t have the helper available, you can eyeball the repo – it’s a Node.js project.)

```bash
# Analyse the repo (this is just a demonstration – replace with your own tool if needed)
# The function returns a JSON object with language percentages.
# Example output: {"JavaScript": 95.3, "JSON": 2.1, "Markdown": 2.6}
```

### 2.2 Create a Dockerfile

Create a minimal Dockerfile that uses the official Node.js LTS image, copies the source, installs dependencies and starts the app.

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package.json & lockfile first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:20-alpine` is small, secure and includes the latest LTS.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees reproducible builds.  
> * Exposing port `3000` matches the default port used by many Node.js starter projects.

### 2.3 Create Kubernetes YAML files

Below is a simple deployment + service that runs 2 replicas of the container and exposes it via a `ClusterIP` service.

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # Update with your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
# k8s/service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # Service port
    targetPort: 3000  # Container port
```

> **Tip:** If you want to expose the service externally, change `type: ClusterIP` to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer`.

### 2.4 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Add a `.github/workflows/ci.yml` file that builds the Docker image, pushes it to Docker Hub (or any registry you prefer), and optionally runs tests.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest

    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test
```

> **Prerequisites**  
> * Add `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` and `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` secrets to the repo settings.  
> * Adjust the image tag (`zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`) if you’re using a different registry.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new files

```bash
# Stage the new artefacts
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml k8s/service.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

> If you want to keep the `k8s` folder separate, create it first:

```bash
mkdir -p k8s
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
# Commit the changes
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests and CI workflow"

# Push to the remote repo
git push origin main
```

---

## Quick sanity check

After pushing, you should see:

* A new `Dockerfile` at the repo root.  
* A `k8s/` directory containing `deployment.yaml` and `service.yaml`.  
* A `.github/workflows/ci.yml` file that triggers on pushes to `main`.  
* The GitHub Actions tab should show a successful run (once the secrets are set).

---

### What if you’re running this in a CI pipeline?

If you’re executing these steps inside a CI job that already has the repo checked out, just skip the `git clone` part and start from step 2.  
Make sure the CI runner has write access to the repo (e.g., via a personal access token or SSH key) so that `git push` succeeds.

Happy coding! 🚀
